Player Primer

The Shattered Sea, 1495 DR: sixty thousand square miles of reef, deep channel, cliff port, free harbour, lost ruin, colonial ledger, old god, hungry storm, and ships with too many secrets in the hold. Magic here is part of the infrastructure — enchanted instruments, divine tribute systems, ruins still running on power no one has claimed, and magic treated the same way everything else is treated out here: as leverage.

This is a sandbox campaign about sailing past the edges of the map. You will bargain with captains who smile while counting your exits, dodge patrol officers who treat extortion as paperwork, hear prayers muttered into saltwater before every voyage, and learn which islands welcome strangers only because they have not decided what to charge yet.

The sea is beautiful. The sea is expensive. The sea remembers.

What Kind of Story Is This?

TLDR: Seen Archer? That but Age of Sail High Magic DnD with some Renaissance punk vibes

The Shattered Sea is swashbuckling, dangerous, and a little rotten under the polish. Warships fly lacquered pennants over holds full of stolen cargo. Merchant princes speak softly because they already own the room. Priests of Umberlee bless ships with one hand and count tribute with the other. Pirates, smugglers, clerks, monks, hunters, spies, and deserters all use the same docks because out here everyone needs passage eventually.

Expect:

  • Nautical exploration across islands, reefs, storms, trenches, and contested ports.
  • High magic in practical hands: enchanted instruments, divine tribute, old ruins, ship upgrades, strange species, and magic treated as part of the economy.
  • Colonial pressure without a clean map of good and evil. Institutions want taxes, leverage, obedience, labour, souls, or silence. Individuals inside them may want something smaller and messier.
  • Ancient mysteries visible at the edges: impossible stone, wrong currents, missing ships, old records, and sailors who refuse to say what they saw east of the charts.
  • Player-driven trouble. There is no single correct route. Your alliances, grudges, bargains, and mistakes are the plot.

The Sea Itself

Two hard boundaries define the Scatter. To the west, the Galewall. To the east, the Drowned Maw. Between them, everything else.

The air changes before land appears: warm, salt-heavy, green with rainforest carried over the water. Then the islands rise in pieces: pale limestone, black basalt, dark jungle, reef water bright enough to hurt your eyes, and deep channels where the colour drops away all at once.

The main island chain is the Verdant Scatter, running between the Galewall and the Drowned Maw in two arcs: the larger, more administered Crown Islands to the north and the denser, harder-to-govern Midchain to the south. Between them runs the Central Strait, the main trade route of the region.

The Galewall

To the west stands the Galewall, a permanent tropical storm belt between the Scatter and the colonial homelands. It appears first as a dark line across the horizon, then as stacked grey weather systems with cold water underneath and wind that builds in stages.

Crossing it takes about three weeks with an experienced pilot. Everyone knows a ship that did not make it. For most sailors, the Galewall is not a route. It is a dare with a fee attached.

The Crown Islands

The northern arc is made of five broad, mountainous islands with forested highlands, deep natural harbours, reef systems, and Dravosi flags at every major anchorage. The islands are rich enough to feed cities and steep enough to fortify, which is why the colonial powers have never stopped caring about them.

Publicly, the Crown Islands mean administration: ratings, inspections, port fees, naval patrols, trade houses, and harbours where authority has a uniform. They are safer than the Midchain in the way a locked room is safer than an open road.

Port Tidefall

Port Tidefall is the Dravosi fortress-port at the western mouth of the Central Strait, carved directly into the cliff face of Calder’s Tooth. The city rises in tiers: Dockfront at the waterline, the Shelf mid-cliff, and Fort Crestwall above with cannon looking seaward.

This is where the Crown’s authority is loudest and most negotiable. Every ship entering the Strait is expected to submit to inspection. The Harbourmaster’s Office sells charts and ratings; the Waveservants keep a shrine near the waterline; and the gallows at the harbour gate make sure nobody mistakes bureaucracy for softness.

Calveno

Calveno is the oldest commercial centre in the Scatter: a canal city of pale stone facades, flat-bottomed boats, public negotiations, and private debts. There are no docks in the ordinary sense. Boats thread through channels cut between buildings, and the sound of the city is a thousand conversations happening at once in the open.

Everything here is visible. That is the point. Deals are witnessed, alliances are performed, and the right association seen by the right people can matter as much as the cargo itself. The Tessarine Concordat has deep roots here, as does the Rattkin Passage.

The Central Strait

The Central Strait is the broad corridor of pale blue-green water between the Crown Islands and the Midchain. It runs forty to eighty miles wide depending on where you cross, deep enough for the largest vessels in the region and sheltered enough that smaller ships use it constantly.

This is the Scatter’s main east-west highway. The current pushes east whether you want it to or not, spinner dolphins work the shipping lanes, and Dravosi inspection at the western mouth makes the Strait profitable before a single cargo changes hands.

The Midchain

The southern arc is dozens of small and medium islands packed close together: limestone, coral, jungle, reef, hidden channels, and local arrangements that do not survive contact with paperwork. Most islands are a half-day’s sail from the next. Fresh water, shelter, and trouble are always nearby.

The Midchain is difficult to govern from outside. Colonial powers hold strategic points and send patrols through the channels, but most of the region belongs to island groups, free ports, smugglers, pilots, family networks, and whoever knows the reef better than the person chasing them. Kalowe as well as the Verdant Teeth both call the midchain home.

Kalowe

Kalowe is the primary Midchain free port, built across three reef islands over a natural lagoon. The reef breaks the swells, the harbour water lies mirror-flat, and the dry dock cranes are the first thing visible above the treeline on approach.

If Port Tidefall is where papers become chains, Kalowe is where papers become optional. It is the standard port for unregistered vessels, black-market cargo, crew-for-hire, ship repairs, and people who need to become harder to find. It has no colonial authority, which is not the same thing as having no politics.

The Verdant Teeth

Two days south-west of Kalowe sit the Verdant Teeth, five closely grouped islands held by Grung clans. From the water they read as dense rainforest, low reef-fringed coasts, and elevated limestone ridges hidden under canopy. Charts mark the interiors with some version of “do not approach.”

Outsiders trade at designated beaches and stay at the waterline. The Grung touch is poisonous, their caste protocols are strict, and the coastal settlements of the Midchain know that raid activity has worsened. Everyone has heard enough to avoid the interior. Some merchants still go to the beach for the lucrative trade opportunities.

The Tail

The Tail is where both arcs of the Scatter narrow toward the Drowned Maw. The islands grow fewer, taller, colder, and more wind-exposed. High cliffs drop straight to deep water, morning fog burns off by midday, and the sea takes on a harder colour near the shelf edge.

This is Maw-adjacent country: longline grounds, serious pilots, salvage staging, cliff communities, and people who have lived close enough to the trench to stop treating unease as useful information. From here, the east stops feeling like direction and starts feeling like depth.

The Drowned Maw

To the east lies the Drowned Maw, a vast deep-sea trench where compasses drift, sound carries strangely, and the water turns dark long before the horizon changes. Sailors cross it regularly. Most have no trouble. The ones who do have trouble tend to become warnings rather than sources.

The Maw is not forbidden. Nothing so simple. Ships go there for salvage, pilgrimage, research, desperation, and profit. The Sentinels of the Eyrie watch it from the High Eyrie. The Waveservants do not like questions about it. Every chart grows less confident near the edge.

The Outer Reach and Sunken Crown

East of the Maw, the charts thin out into open ocean. The Outer Reach has no colonial presence, no reliable resupply, and few landmarks a western pilot would trust. Getting there means crossing the Maw and then committing to days of open water.

The best-known region beyond is the Sunken Crown: five low islands around a deep blue hole, black stone and pale reef around water that drops too cleanly to be comfortable. It is associated with old Umberlee worship, isolated Tabaxi communities, and local navigation that outsiders routinely underestimate.

Powers on the Water

  • The Dravosi Crown controls much of the Crown Islands through naval force, fortress ports, and a bureaucracy that treats paperwork like divine law. Resistance becomes “administrative non-compliance,” and administrative non-compliance can become cannon fire once properly filed.

  • The Tessarine Concordat prefers leverage to conquest. Its factors dress plainly, speak warmly, and always know the current price of what you are carrying. They do not need to seize a city if they can own it.

  • The Passage is the Rattkin network beneath and between the ports: runs, holds, courier routes, hidden caches, and spoken in skitter-cant, a completely silent language of nose and whisker movement.

  • The Grung Clans hold the rainforest interiors of the Verdant Teeth in the Midchain. Coastal islanders trade at designated beaches and do not go inland. Everyone knows Grung touch is poisonous. Everyone knows the slave raids have been getting worse.

  • Umberlee and the Waveservants are the religious fact of life at sea. Umberlee, often called the Bitch Queen of the Sea, is the goddess of storms, shipwrecks, and the sea’s destructive appetite. Her Waveservants keep shrines at port entries, their robes smell of tallow and brine, and their blessings are transactional by design. They collect tribute from everyone. Sailors who do not pay do not sail, or at least do not sail confidently.

  • The Sentinels of the Eyrie are an Aarakocra monastic order watching the Drowned Maw from high basalt stone. They are not a navy, not a church, and not a government. They observe, record, and keep recording when everyone else starts arguing about what the records mean. The High Eyrie is their basalt sea-stack monastery near the northeastern Crown coast. Visitors are rare, the practical approach is aerial, and its ledgers are understood to be the most complete Maw observation record in the Scatter.

Peoples of the Shattered Sea

Most species from the 2024 sourcebooks have a place in the Scatter. The following homebrew options are native to the setting:

  • Grung: amphibious, poisonous, caste-shaped survivors of a harsh society. A Grung PC should be ready to define what they believe about the order they came from.
  • Rattkin: small, flexible, hard to catch, and native to the hidden infrastructure of port life. Rattkin make excellent smugglers, scouts, couriers, spies, sailors, and people who were definitely not in that locked room.
  • Tabaxi: feline humanoids with ancient roots in the Shattered Sea, especially among the isolated island tribes of the Sunken Crown.
  • Aarakocra: winged people whose relationship to height, distance, and danger is fundamentally different from ground-bound folk.

If you want to play something stranger, ask. The Shattered Sea has room for oddities, but the character still needs a reason to stay with the crew.

Ships, Home, and Upgrades

Your vessel is not just transportation. It is shelter, leverage, reputation, storage, escape route, and eventually home.

Once the ship is yours, it operates as a combined Ship Bastion: the 2024 Bastion rules adapted for a mobile vessel.

  • Facility slots are pooled across the party.
  • Weekly Bastion Turns handle upkeep, crew wages, facility orders, repairs, trade, visitors, and maritime events.
  • Ship size matters. A sloop cannot hold the same life, guns, cargo, and magical infrastructure as a frigate. See Ship Stats for the tier system.

Early on, expect to think like sailors even before you own the deck under your feet. Crew, cargo, water, repairs, charts, port fees, bribes, and grudges all matter.

The Starting Situation

You begin at Level 3 aboard the Saltwright.

A hard-used two-masted merchant brig captained by Beaumont Sel, who offered you passage to Port Tidefall

You might be a paying passenger, a working hand, a shipwrecked survivor, a stowaway, a fugitive, a pilgrim, a hired blade, a scholar with bad funding, etc. Whatever brought you aboard, the Saltwright is where your stories collide.

Character Creation

  • Use D&D 2024 rules by default. 2014 material is allowed if adapted cleanly to 2024.
  • Start at Level 3.
  • Roll stats with 4d6 drop lowest. You may roll three arrays; if you hate all three, use point buy.
  • Take standard starting equipment plus one uncommon magic item from your previous adventures.
  • Official sourcebook content is static. Homebrew or adjusted content may be tuned during play if balance gets weird.
  • Powerful, strange, optimized, comedic, or highly specific builds are welcome. The one hard requirement: make a character with some reason to work with the party.
  • Character death is possible. The DM will not aim to kill you, but the sea, the dice, and your decisions will not be padded. Death will be treated with narrative weight, and resurrection or a new same-level character are both on the table.

Optional: The Mortis System

A Mortis is a Session Zero option that pairs a permanent mechanical drawback with a targeted mechanical benefit. It is not a curse and not a punishment. It is a fact about your character expressed through mechanics: the same truth that limits them also makes them exceptional.

Mortises require DM approval and lock in at Session Zero.

2024 system for combining multiple spellcasters to empower a single spell via Augment, Distribute, Expand, or Prolong options; no resource cost beyond spell slots and actions.

# Circle Magic

Multiple spellcasters combine efforts to empower a single spell. Introduced in *Heroes of Faerun* (2024). No resource cost beyond spell slots and Actions.

> [!dm]
> Extremely powerful and potentially game-breaking. Limit by keeping NPC spellcasters rare or unhelpful — even level 1 NPC Wizards acting as Secondary Casters dramatically amplify the party's output.

## How It Works

1. The **primary caster** takes the Magic action and begins casting a qualifying spell (casting time of one Action or 1+ minutes — no Reactions or Bonus Actions).
2. Primary caster selects a **Circle Casting Option** (see below).
3. **Secondary casters** are identified. Must have the Spellcasting or Pact Magic feature. Species traits and feat-based spells do not qualify.
4. Each secondary caster takes the Magic action on their turn to empower the spell (spending a spell slot if required by the option).
5. When the **final secondary caster** takes the Magic action, the spell takes effect.

Primary caster must maintain Concentration throughout. No stated time limit — the process can span multiple turns.

## Circle Casting Options

Only one option is selected per casting.

**Augment.** Adds 1,000 ft. to the spell's range, up to a 1-mile maximum. Spells with a Self range are unaffected. Applies to the range value, not the area in parentheses.

**Distribute.** Transfers Concentration on the spell to a willing secondary caster. Primary caster may then maintain Concentration on a different spell. The spell continues until any one Concentrating caster drops it.

**Expand.** Increases the area of a spell. Secondary casters expend a spell slot (any level) to contribute. No stated maximum area increase.

**Prolong.** Extends the spell's duration by 1 hour per secondary caster, up to 24 hours. Secondary casters expend a spell slot (any level). Most powerful on non-Concentration spells (Mage Armor, Blink, Mirror Image, Fire Shield, Foresight).

**Safeguard.** Excludes designated 5-ft. squares from the spell's area of effect. Allows party members to be safely inside an area spell. Works on ongoing spells (Wall of Fire, Hunger of Hadar).

**Supplant.** Secondary casters expend a spell slot of equal or higher level to reduce the spell's gp material component cost (50 gp per secondary caster). No secondary casters needed for spells without gp components.

## Circle Spells and Metamagic

Metamagic can be combined with Circle Casting Options. Interaction order for mathematical changes to range or duration is ambiguous in the rules — adjudicate at the table.

# Rival Team Design

Pointy Hat's method for creating rival parties as foils to player characters. Requires PCs to be finalized first.

## What Is a Foil?

A foil highlights another character's traits by contrasting with them. Two methods:

- **Opposite foil** — every key trait is inverted. Simpler to create; high immediate impact.
- **Mirror foil** — shares most traits with the PC, but one or more key aspects are flipped to maximize contrast. More nuanced; better for rivals who feel genuinely parallel.

## The Four Steps

### Step I: Examine the Hero

Boil each PC down to three categories:

- **Character Traits** — personality attributes
- **Backstory Information** — formative history
- **Want** — the core driving desire

### Step II: Choose Foil Type

Pick opposite or mirror. Mirror foils are recommended for rival teams — they feel more personal.

### Step III: Create the Rival

Apply the same three categories to the rival, flipping only the elements that create the most friction or contrast. Keep shared elements to make the parallel legible.

*Example: A PC wants to live up to impossible expectations (anxiety, warmth, scrappiness). Their mirror rival has the same drive but nobody expects anything from them — determined and cold, fighting for recognition while the PC fights to survive expectation.*

Rival Team Design

Pointy Hat’s method for creating rival parties as foils to player characters. Requires PCs to be finalized first.

What Is a Foil?

A foil highlights another character’s traits by contrasting with them. Two methods:

  • Opposite foil — every key trait is inverted. Simpler to create; high immediate impact.
  • Mirror foil — shares most traits with the PC, but one or more key aspects are flipped to maximize contrast. More nuanced; better for rivals who feel genuinely parallel.

The Four Steps

Step I: Examine the Hero

Boil each PC down to three categories:

  • Character Traits — personality attributes
  • Backstory Information — formative history
  • Want — the core driving desire

Step II: Choose Foil Type

Pick opposite or mirror. Mirror foils are recommended for rival teams — they feel more personal.

Step III: Create the Rival

  • Give the rival team a similar motivation (same goal type, not same objective) — creates natural collision.

Large-scale combat overlay for armies, enormous monsters, or conflicts too large for standard 5e. Adds a Siege Phase at initiative count 20.

# Siege Rules

A combat overlay for battles where normal 5e combat cannot represent the scale: armies besieging a fortress, enormous monsters attacking a city, or conflicts with too many participants to run individually. Does not replace character combat — adds a large-scale **Siege Phase** at initiative count 20, resolving before lair actions.

## Core Procedure

- Each side has AC, HP, attack bonus, damage bonus, abilities, and Siege Actions.
- Siege Phase happens at initiative count 20 (wins ties, before lair actions).
- At the start of each Siege Phase, each party rolls 1d20. Higher roll chooses and resolves a Siege Action first; lower roll follows. Alternate until both sides have used their available actions.
- Each party can take up to 3 Siege Actions per Siege Phase.
- Each Siege Action can be used only once per round.
- GM chooses enemy Siege Actions. Players collectively choose allied Siege Actions.
- **Siege Attack Actions:** deal damage on hit; half damage on miss.
- **Siege Effect Actions:** apply debuff or disable on hit; no effect on miss (limited uses not consumed).
- Natural 20s do not double Siege damage dice.

## Initiative Order with Siege Phase

1. Creatures above initiative 20 act.
2. Siege Phase resolves.
3. One available lair action resolves (if applicable).
4. Creatures below initiative 20 act.

## Design Notes

Siege rules work best when:

- The party's individual actions can meaningfully affect the siege totals (disabling siege actions, protecting key NPCs).
- Named NPC deaths have mechanical weight (Blaze of Glory: their last action resolves immediately before they die).
- The encounter's end state is not "kill everything" but a specific objective (ritual completed, creature retreats, city saves).

> [!dm]
> Source: Pointy Hat's "Storm Rising" adventure. The specific stat blocks in the source (Cape Coral, Kraken, etc.) are for that adventure. Use the procedure above to build Shattered Sea siege blocks when needed.

# Sports Match Rules

5e-based rules for running a sports match as a combat encounter. The sport itself is intentionally vague — flavor it to fit the setting. Share with players the session before the match.

## Core Rules

- Goal: score more points within the time limit.
- A match lasts **10 rounds** (or 20 for a longer match).
- Score by shooting the ball into the enemy goal.
- A **15-foot-radius Goal Zone** surrounds each goal. Only the goalie may enter it.
- Each team designates one **goalie** who cannot leave the Goal Zone.
- After a goal: defending goalie takes control, all players return to starting positions, match continues.
- **Tie-breaker:** Three penalty shots per team.

## Actions

**Pass** *(Action)* — Pass to a teammate up to 30 feet. Dexterity attack + proficiency vs DC 10.

**Shoot** *(Action)* — Launch toward the goal (max 30 feet). Strength attack + proficiency determines distance traveled (10–30 ft on roll of 10–26+).

**Tackle** *(Action)* — Force carrier to drop ball and push 10 feet. Strength (Athletics) contested by Athletics or Acrobatics.

**Steal** *(Action)* — Take the ball without force. Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) vs Insight or Acrobatics.

## Bonus Actions

**Pick Up** *(Bonus Action)* — Pick up a ball within 5 feet when not in any creature's possession.

## Reactions

**Intercept** *(Reaction)* — Stop a pass/shot through your reach. Dexterity save vs passer's/shooter's roll; success gains possession.

**Lunge** *(Reaction)* — Move up to 10 feet in any direction except during your own turn.

## Concentration Rule

If a ball-carrier takes any damage, they make a Concentration save. On failure, they drop the ball.

## Role Guide

| Role | Best Build |
|---|---|
| Goalie | High Dexterity; ranged combatant |
| Defender | Casters; stay near goalie to maximize range |
| Midfielder | Dexterity-based; facilitate passes |
| Attacker | Strength-based; the only way to score is a Shoot action |

## Connections

- [[siege-rules|Siege Rules]] — another large-scale rules overlay

# Villain Design Framework

Pointy Hat's system-agnostic villain creation method. Three principles, each starting with "P."

## I — Active (Has Agency)

The villain must have a **goal** that is obtainable but campaign-spanning, with clear actionable steps the villain takes and players can interrupt. The villain must also react to player interference with counter-moves.

**Design questions:** What does the villain want? How will they pursue it step by step? How can players interrupt each step? How can the villain respond to those interruptions?

**Worked example:** Villain wants to resurrect their dead lover → must sacrifice four of the lover's living descendants → players can hide, protect, or fake the death of descendants → villain can infiltrate their refuge, deceive players into protecting the wrong person, or manipulate a descendant into willing sacrifice.

## II — Present (Has Visibility)

The villain must interact with the party semi-regularly — not just a final boss. Players need to form an emotional relationship with the villain.

**Ways to make a villain present without lethal confrontations:**

- An item that lets players communicate with the villain.
- The villain appears only as an illusion (physically trapped elsewhere).
- Political context means the villain can't attack openly without jeopardizing their own plans.
- The villain doesn't want to kill the party — they want to use or redirect them.
- The villain can only manifest under limited conditions.
- The villain is subtly steering the party to accomplish the villain's goal for them.

## III — Personal (Has Stakes)

The party must have a personal reason to stop the villain beyond "it's the right thing to do."

**Ways to create personal stakes:**

- Shared history (family, mentor/pupil, past betrayal).
- The villain usurped something that belongs to a PC.
- The PC trained under the villain and they formed a master-pupil bond.
- The villain's existence directly threatens a PC's way of life.
- The villain controls or has deceived someone close to a PC.
- The villain's goal would destroy something a PC cares about.

**If the villain can't be tied to all PCs:** give the villain a second-in-command with a personal connection to remaining PCs.

Pointy Hat's system for dynamic boss fights: the boss telegraphs a threat at end of its turn, players have a full round to neutralize or mitigate it before resolution.

# Battlefield Actions

Pointy Hat's system for making boss fights dynamic. Each Battlefield Action shifts the players' objective away from pure damage-dealing for one full initiative round. Boss-only — never assign to minions or two monsters in the same encounter.

## How They Work

Every Battlefield Action has exactly two phases:

**Tell** — Announced at the *end* of the boss's turn. No damage. A vivid cue telegraphing what is coming and how to stop it.

**Resolution** — Triggers at the *start* of the boss's next turn. Players have the full initiative order between Tell and Resolution to respond.

Each action is either:

- **Neutralized** — players fully stop the effect
- **Mitigated** — players reduce but cannot prevent the effect

Give a boss at least 2 Battlefield Actions so the action rotates each round.

## Damage by CR

| Boss CR | BA Damage |
|---|---|
| 3–9 | 3d10 |
| 10–16 | 9d10 |
| 17–23 | 11d10 |
| 24+ | 13d10 |

**Optional:** Use the monster's highest single-action damage instead for a less punishing variant.

**Save DC:** `8 + key ability modifier + Proficiency Bonus`

Damage type is determined by the monster's identity. Never leave damage type ambiguous.

## Canonical BA Templates

### Summoning Minions

**Tell:** Two 10-foot-radius summoning circles appear on the battlefield. The faint outline of a monster begins to coalesce within each.

**Neutralization:** A creature stepping on a circle stops that minion from being summoned.

**Resolution:** If not neutralized, two minions are summoned to assist the boss.

---

### Cleave

**Tell:** The boss raises its weapon, readying a devastating attack. Whenever a creature deals damage to the boss, it faces that creature — changing the Cleave's area of effect.

**Mitigation:** A hardy character holds their attack until just before the boss's turn, ensuring the Cleave targets them. A ranged combatant hits last while others clear the cone. A rogue hits, disengages, and runs.

**Resolution:** The boss Cleaves a 15-foot cone in the direction it's facing. Each creature in the area makes a Dexterity save — full damage on failure, half on success.

---

### Ray

**Tell:** The boss coalesces magical energy into a ball on its palm. Whenever a creature deals damage to the boss, it faces that creature — changing the ray's direction.

**Mitigation:** A hardy character holds their attack until just before the boss's turn to redirect the ray toward themselves.

**Resolution:** A 5-foot-wide, 60-foot-long ray fires in the direction the boss faces. Each creature in the path makes a Dexterity save — full damage on failure, half on success.

---

### Enchanting Ballad

**Tell:** The boss enters deep concentration and begins a haunting melody.

**Neutralization:** Break the boss's Concentration as normal, or use *Silence*.

**Resolution:** The creature with the lowest Wisdom score that can hear the song gains the Charmed condition until the song ends. It may repeat the save at the end of each of its turns.

---

### Watchful Eye

**Tell:** The boss opens its eyes; dreadful magical energy gathers in its pupil.

**Neutralization:** Players must not be visible to the boss when Resolution triggers. Options: use the environment to block line of sight, take the Hide action, cast *Darkness*.

**Resolution:** All creatures the boss can see gain the Frightened condition. They may make a Wisdom save at the end of each of their turns to end the effect.

---

### Perfect Illusion

**Tell:** The boss creates three illusory copies of itself. Each copy begins to gather magical energy.

**Neutralization:** Illusory copies share the boss's ability scores and AC but have only 1 HP. Players must destroy them before the boss's next turn.

**Resolution:** Each surviving copy makes one attack against a creature, using an attack from the boss's stat block (not BA damage).

---

### Tactical Retreat

**Tell:** The boss concentrates on a spell; its form begins to slowly dematerialize.

**Neutralization:** Break the boss's Concentration as normal.

**Resolution:** If not neutralized, the boss teleports to a location of its choice, escaping the battle.

---

### Danse Macabre

**Tell:** The boss begins an enchanting dance.

**Neutralization:** Break the boss's Concentration as normal, or reduce the boss's speed to 0.

**Resolution:** All creatures hostile to the boss are under the effects of *Irresistible Dance* until the end of their next turn.

---

### Eruption

**Tell:** The boss punches the ground; cracks snake outward from the impact. Energy shines brightest at the epicenter.

**Mitigation:** Players must move as far as possible from the impact point.

**Resolution:** Creatures within 20 feet make a Dexterity save — full damage on failure, half on success. Creatures 25+ feet away make a Dexterity save — half damage on failure, none on success.

---

### Eye of the Hurricane

**Tell:** The boss generates a massive wind vortex centered on itself. The only calm zone is directly adjacent to the boss.

**Mitigation:** Players must move as close to the boss as possible.

**Resolution:** Creatures more than 10 feet from the boss make a Dexterity save — full damage and pushed 30 feet away on failure, half damage and pushed 15 feet on success. Creatures within 10 feet make a Dexterity save — half damage and pushed 15 feet on failure, no damage on success.

---

## Design Notes

- Mix action types: at least one that forces movement, one that targets Concentration.
- Too many movement-forcing actions can feel obstructive; too many Concentration-targeting actions feel repetitive.
- Adapt templates with monster-specific flavor; original actions are preferred when the monster has strong thematic identity.

Session zero character option pairing a permanent mechanical drawback (the Mark) with a targeted benefit (the Gift) — a character's limitation and strength express the same concept.

# The Mortis

> *A Mortis is never a punishment. It is a fact about who the character is, expressed through mechanics.*

A session zero option pairing a permanent mechanical disadvantage (the **Mark**) with a targeted mechanical benefit (the **Gift**). The two sides always describe the same person — not a character who is also cursed, but a character whose strengths and limits are two sides of the same coin.

## Design Rules

**Mark and Gift describe the same person.** Read only the Mark — you should still be able to sketch the character.

**The Mark must have real teeth.** Must apply consistently in situations that come up at this table.

**The Gift must target the core fantasy.** Not a consolation prize — the thing that makes the character feel more like themselves.

**The Gift always exceeds the Mark in value.** At maximum punishing Mark, the Gift reaches roughly the value of a free feat.

## Creating a Mortis

1. Player names the character flaw — a fact that limits them in a specific, consistent way
2. DM translates it into a specific mechanical condition
3. DM proposes a Gift that exceeds the Mark and targets the player fantasy
4. Both agree. It locks in. DM has final say on both sides.

**One Mortis per character. Does not change as the character levels.**

## What Makes a Bad Mortis

- A Mark that barely triggers (free feat in disguise)
- A Gift that misses the player fantasy
- A Mark punishing a core class feature
- A Mark requiring case-by-case adjudication

## The Party's Mortises

### The Small — [[perrin-black-jaw|Perrin Black-Jaw]]

Not built to haul rope or take a hit in a scrum — so he leads instead.

- **Mark:** Disadvantage on all Strength-based checks and saving throws.
- **Gift:** Charisma score increases by 2.

### The Unmasked — [[jean-claude-tabarnack|Jean-Claude Tabarnack]]

What he is reads clearly — in his face, in his stillness, in how he positions before a fight.

- **Mark:** Disadvantage on Charisma (Persuasion) and Charisma (Deception) checks.
- **Gift:** Advantage on Wisdom (Perception) and Wisdom (Survival) checks.

### The Crowded — [[delmar-fisk|Delmar Fisk]]

Five captains' souls pressed into him by Umberlee as the fleet sank.

- **Mark:** Disadvantage on all Wisdom saving throws. When a captain's trigger fires, that captain surfaces involuntarily.
- **Gift:** Once per short rest (bonus action), surface one captain. While surfaced, gain that captain's skill proficiencies as borrowed mastery; if already proficient, gain Expertise instead. The brass flagon returns Delmar to the surface from any captain.

# Mounts and Vehicles

## Mounts and Other Animals

A mount helps move more quickly through the wilderness; primary purpose is carrying gear. An animal pulling a vehicle can move weight up to 5× its base carrying capacity.

|---|---|---|
| Axe Beak | 210 lb. | 50 GP |
| Camel | 450 lb. | 50 GP |
| Elephant | 1,320 lb. | 200 GP |

# Optimization Meta (2024 D&D)

DM-facing reference for 2024 5e balance and build optimization. Based on RPGBOT's state-of-meta analysis (December 2025).

## Key Meta Observations

**Martial vs. Caster Disparity.** Unchanged and worsening. Full casters dominate; Conjure Minor Elementals alone lets a Wizard out-damage optimized martial builds.

**Healing in Combat.** Still mostly inefficient. Optimal play: let an ally fall to 0, then revive with Healing Word. Never spend slots preemptively on healing.

**Forced Movement.** Extremely prevalent in 2024. Weapon Mastery (Push), Grappler feat, and class features all offer it from level 1. Dragging creatures into hazards or off ledges is broadly viable.

**Circle Casting.** See [[circle-magic|Circle Magic]]. Broken. Limit by keeping NPC spellcasters rare.

**Grappling.** Changed in 2024 — Grapple uses STR/DEX Athletics vs. STR/DEX Save. No longer imposes Restrained; just reduces speed to 0. Combined with Weapon Mastery (Push/Topple) to trigger Prone, then attack with Advantage.

---

## Best of the Meta

| Category | Best Pick | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Background | **Scribe** | Skilled feat; Investigation + Perception covers most non-combat needs |
| Class | **Wizard** (or Cleric) | Full spellcasters dominate; all top 5 are full casters |
| Origin Feat | **Musician** | Heroic Inspiration for 2–6 party members; whole-party force multiplier |
| Epic Boon | **Boon of Fate** | +/- 2d4 on any D20 Test; offensive or defensive |
| Multiclass Dip | **Cleric / Fighter / Paladin** | Each grants Con saves, heavy armor, or both |

## Worst of the Meta

| Category | Worst Pick | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Background | **Artisan** | Narrow spread; Persuasion useless to most builds; Crafter feat is weak |
| Class | **Ranger** | Locked into Hunter's Mark; limits build diversity |
| Origin Feat | **Crafter** | 20% discount on nonmagical items; gold rarely matters after early levels |

# Aberrant Sorcery

*Sorcerer subclass — Player's Handbook (2024)*

Psionic power derived from alien influence: a psychic wind from the Astral Plane, Far Realm exposure, or an unfinished mind flayer transformation.

---

## Features

**Psionic Spells (Level 3).** Always-prepared spells by level:

- 3: Arms of Hadar, Calm Emotions, Detect Thoughts, Dissonant Whispers, Mind Sliver
- 5: Hunger of Hadar, Sending
- 7: Evard's Black Tentacles, Summon Aberration
- 9: Rary's Telepathic Bond, Telekinesis

**Telepathic Speech (Level 3).** Bonus Action: telepathic link with one visible creature within 30 feet. Lasts Sorcerer level in minutes, range = CHA mod in miles (min 1).

**Psionic Sorcery (Level 6).** Cast any Psionic Spell by spending SP equal to spell level instead of a slot. Requires no Verbal, Somatic, or non-consumed Material components when cast this way.

**Psychic Defenses (Level 6).** Resistance to Psychic damage. Advantage on saves vs. Charmed or Frightened.

**Revelation in Flesh (Level 14).** Bonus Action: spend 1+ SP to gain physical alterations for 10 minutes (Aquatic Adaptation, Glistening Flight, See the Invisible, or Wormlike Movement per point spent).

**Warping Implosion (Level 18).** Magic action: teleport 120 feet, then all creatures within 30 feet of departure point make STR save (spell DC) — fail: 3d10 Force + pulled to empty space; success: half. 1/LR; costs 5 SP to restore.

# Arcane Trickster

*Rogue subclass — Player's Handbook (2024)*

## Features

**Spellcasting (Level 3).** INT-based (Wizard list). Sneak Attack applies only to Finesse/ranged weapon attacks, not spell attacks.

**Versatile Trickster (Level 13).** Use your Mage Hand to impose Disadvantage on attacks vs. you (Bonus Action) and grant advantage on your next attack vs. the same target.

**Spell Thief (Level 17).** After a creature within 30 ft. casts a spell of 4th level or lower, you can use your Reaction to force a save — on failure, they forget the spell and you prepare it instead for 8 hours.

2024 rules for player-owned strongholds; characters gain a Bastion at level 5 and issue orders to its special facilities every 7 in-game days.

# Bastions

A Bastion is a location owned by a player character: a home, stronghold, or place of power that develops over a campaign. It provides refuge, and its facilities can craft magic items, conduct research, harvest poisons, build ships, and more.

## Gaining a Bastion

Characters acquire Bastions at **level 5**. Shape, style, and function are the player's choice. Multiple characters can combine Bastions into a single structure.

## Bastion Turns

A Bastion turn occurs every **7 days of in-game time**, whether or not the character is present. On each turn, a character issues orders to their Bastion's special facilities, or issues Maintain to the whole Bastion.

## Basic Facilities

Every Bastion starts with **two free basic facilities** (1 Cramped, 1 Roomy, player's choice):

Bedroom · Dining Room · Parlor · Courtyard · Stable · Storage · Well/Cistern

## Facility Space

| Space | Maximum Area |
|---|---|
| Cramped | 4 squares |
| Roomy | 16 squares |
| Vast | 36 squares |

## Orders

| Order | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Craft** | Produce items, magic items, or written works |
| **Trade** | Buy or sell goods; generates GP income |
| **Harvest** | Gather herbs, poisons, creature products |
| **Research** | Gather information, discover lore |
| **Recruit** | Hire Bastion Defenders or recruit agents |
| **Empower** | Grant magical benefits to self or allies |
| **Maintain** | Keep the Bastion running; triggers Bastion Events roll |

## Combining Bastions

Two or more characters can combine their Bastions into one structure. Each character retains their own facility slots, hirelings, and orders. Bastion Defenders can be shared to absorb losses across the combined structure.

## Mobile Bastions

A Bastion can be built into a vehicle (ship, airship, lightning rail). Mobile Bastions cannot have defensive walls. The [[hcs-surety|Uncertainty]] serves as the party's mobile Bastion.

## Bastion Defenders

Hirelings who defend the Bastion. On an Attack event, roll 6d6; each 1 kills one Defender. If Defenders reach 0, a random special facility shuts down for one Bastion turn.

**RPGBOT note:** Defenders are a trap — the cost to maintain them usually exceeds their value. Defensive Walls (250 GP per 5-ft square, 10 days each) reduce attack dice by 2 and are generally more cost-effective.

## Fall of a Bastion

A Bastion is lost by Divestiture (voluntary), Neglect (no orders for a number of turns equal to character level), or Ruination. A new Bastion can always be established afterward.

# Ship Combat

Expands the **2024 DMG vehicle rules**. Covers movement, chases, ramming, and campaign-specific gun rules.

---

## Ship Movement

**Helm action.** A creature acting as helmsman uses their action to move the ship up to its speed. The ship can turn up to 90 degrees before, during, or after this movement; each 90-degree turn costs 5 feet of movement. A ship cannot move backward.

---

## Chases

Ships move on their turns in initiative order. A helmsman can Dash to move the ship its speed a second time. Each round compare total distance covered — if the pursuer outpaces the quarry, the gap closes by the difference. Roll a d20 for Chase Complications at the start of each participant's turn.

**Escape:** The quarry escapes when the gap exceeds 500 feet in open water, or they reach impassable terrain. The pursuer catches up when the gap reaches 0.

---

## Ramming

A ship that moves at least 20 feet in a straight line and ends within 5 feet of another vessel may ram (part of the Helm action).

- Target takes **4d10 bludgeoning damage**.
- **Self-damage by angle:** Striking port/starboard/aft: ramming ship takes 2d10. Fore-to-fore: both take 4d10.
- Target makes DC 15 Strength save; failure: pushed 10 feet.
- Unsecured crew: DC 13 Dexterity save or fall prone and take 1d6.

---

## Gun Crew Requirements

Each gun requires a crew of three.

| Crew | Effect |
|---|---|
| 3 (full) | Fires and reloads normally. Counts as a fully crewed gun. |
| 2 | Reload takes twice as long. Counts as half a gun for damage. |
| 1 | Reload takes three times as long. Half a gun; attack at disadvantage if firing independently. |
| 0 | Cannot fire. |

**Attack:** Ranged attack roll vs target Hull AC. **Hit:** Roll damage. **Miss:** Half damage. **Critical Hit:** Roll damage twice, take higher.

---

## Gunner Actions

A PC filling the **Gunner** role takes one ship action per round:

**Salvo.** Fire all manned guns on one side simultaneously.

1. Choose port or starboard.
2. Roll one attack (Dexterity + proficiency vs Hull AC). Advantage if one Gunner per gun deck.
3. Hit: full damage from all fully crewed guns that side. Miss: half that damage.
4. All guns that fired must reload.

**Aimed Shot.** Fire a single gun at a specific target location (Targeting table below). Uses both the Gunner's ship action and that gun crew's action.

**Reload — All Guns.** Order all gun crews to reload simultaneously (single ship action).

---

## Tier 4 (First-Rate Only)

A Tier 4 ship cannot be matched in direct exchange. **Multi-Deck Salvo:** Roll one attack per deck using Gunner's modifier. Each deck resolves independently. All three decks reload — no full broadside for 3 rounds.

Practical counters: fire ships, shallow water (first-rates draw 25+ ft), fast running escape, multiple fast targets. When the *Sovereign* is an enemy, it is not a combat encounter — it is a situation.

Ship Combat

Expands the 2024 DMG vehicle rules. Covers movement, chases, ramming, and campaign-specific gun rules.

Ship Movement

Helm action. A creature acting as helmsman uses their action to move the ship up to its speed. The ship can turn up to 90 degrees before, during, or after this movement; each 90-degree turn costs 5 feet of movement. A ship cannot move backward.

Chases

Ships move on their turns in initiative order. A helmsman can Dash to move the ship its speed a second time. Each round compare total distance covered — if the pursuer outpaces the quarry, the gap closes by the difference. Roll a d20 for Chase Complications at the start of each participant’s turn.

Escape: The quarry escapes when the gap exceeds 500 feet in open water, or they reach impassable terrain. The pursuer catches up when the gap reaches 0.

Ramming

A ship that moves at least 20 feet in a straight line and ends within 5 feet of another vessel may ram (part of the Helm action).

  • Target takes 4d10 bludgeoning damage.
  • Self-damage by angle: Striking port/starboard/aft: ramming ship takes 2d10. Fore-to-fore: both take 4d10.
  • Target makes DC 15 Strength save; failure: pushed 10 feet.
  • Unsecured crew: DC 13 Dexterity save or fall prone and take 1d6.

Gun Crew Requirements

Each gun requires a crew of three.

CrewEffect
3 (full)Fires and reloads normally. Counts as a fully crewed gun.
2Reload takes twice as long. Counts as half a gun for damage.
1Reload takes three times as long. Half a gun; attack at disadvantage if firing independently.
0Cannot fire.

Attack: Ranged attack roll vs target Hull AC. Hit: Roll damage. Miss: Half damage. Critical Hit: Roll damage twice, take higher.

Gunner Actions

A PC filling the Gunner role takes one ship action per round:

Salvo. Fire all manned guns on one side simultaneously.

  1. Choose port or starboard.
  2. Roll one attack (Dexterity + proficiency vs Hull AC). Advantage if one Gunner per gun deck.
  3. Hit: full damage from all fully crewed guns that side. Miss: half that damage.
  4. All guns that fired must reload.

Aimed Shot. Fire a single gun at a specific target location (Targeting table below). Uses both the Gunner’s ship action and that gun crew’s action.

Reload — All Guns. Order all gun crews to reload simultaneously (single ship action).

|---|---|---|---|

## Navigation Checks

When conditions are uncertain — reef channels, Maw approaches, storms, unfamiliar waters — the Navigator rolls Intelligence (Navigator's Tools).

| DC | Failure |
|---|---|
| 10 | Off course. +1 day. |
| 14 | Significantly off course. +2 days, minor encounter likely. |
| 18 | Lost. +1d4 days, serious complication. |

- Tidewardens' charts grant **advantage** in charted waters.
- Midchain charts are contradictory — no advantage.
- **The Maw:** Compasses fail within 5 miles of the edge. Magical navigation gives false readings. Star navigation is unaffected.

---

## Downtime at Sea

On voyages of 3+ days, characters can perform downtime activities (2024 rules). Activities requiring a specific location or instructor can't be performed at sea.

**Long rests at sea:** If the Cook role is filled, characters recover an additional **1d6 HP**. If a storm hits during rest: DC 12 Constitution save or the rest grants no benefits.

---

## Acquiring a Ship

**Buy.** Available at any port with a shipyard. DC 12 Charisma (Persuasion) to close the typical 10–15% gap from asking price.

**Prize.** Take a ship in combat. Strip a Tier 2 ship for parts: 2,000–4,000 gp at the right buyer.

**Steal.** Tidefall's main harbour is hard. South Harbour on Calder's Tooth's eastern side is loosely administered — ships in the outer bay are accessible by rowboat.

**Mutiny.** Built on crew relationships established beforehand.

**Build.** Same cost as buying new; custom specs possible.

| Tier | Build Time |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2–4 months |
| 2 | 6–12 months |
| 3 | 18–36 months |

---

## Living Quarters by Tier

**Tier 1** — Captain's bunk in the stern, hammocks forward. Party and crew share close quarters.

**Tier 2** — Captain's cabin (private, lockable). Two shared officer berths. Galley. Cargo hold. **Captain's Locker** (DC 18 to break or pick).

**Tier 3** — Officer cabins, wardroom, captain's suite. Full privacy for the party.

---

## Ship Reputation

| Level | Effect |
|---|---|
| Respected | Reduced berth fees. Willing hires. Faction contacts available. |
| Known | Treated on actual deeds. Neutral default. |
| Wanted | Port access restricted or denied. Bounties posted. |
| Notorious | Capable crew seek them out. Some targets surrender rather than fight. |

## Bastion

One shared bastion for the whole party. Slots pool across all PCs. Bastion Turns resolve weekly at sea or in port.

### Levels, Slots & Facility Gates

Both character level and ship tier must be met to install a facility.

| Character Level | Slots/PC | Party Pool (4 PCs) | Unlocks | Min Ship Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Any | — | — | Basic facilities | Any |
| 5 | 2 | 8 | Level 5 facilities | 1 |
| 9 | 3 | 12 | Level 9 facilities | 2 |
| 13 | 4 | 16 | Level 13 facilities | 3 |
| 17 | 5 | 20 | Level 17 facilities | 3 |

### Bastion Turn Orders

| Order | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Craft** | Produce items allowed by the facility. |
| **Empower** | Trigger the facility's power effect. |
| **Harvest** | Collect facility outputs. |
| **Maintain** | No order — roll a Bastion Event. |
| **Recruit** | Hire hirelings, defenders, or specialists. |
| **Research** | Gather intel or identify items. |
| **Trade** | Generate income via commerce. |

Absent PCs need *Sending* to issue orders. No order = Maintain. Neglect kicks in after consecutive missed turns equal to the PC's level.

At-table run guide for Session 0. Covers table norms, character check-ins, Stripes interview, Mortis setup, and party connection. Session 1 is ready to run immediately after.

# Session 00 — Run Guide

**~2–3 hours.** Goal: table norms locked, all five characters established, party aboard the Saltwright with a reason to stay together.

---

## State of Prep

**Ready:**

- Campaign primer, tone, world — fully prepped: [[shattered-sea-tone-guide|Shattered Sea Tone Guide]]
- Gravity wells: Perrin, JC, Delmar, Crissdalynn — complete: [[player-gravity-wells|Player Gravity Wells]]
- Mortises: Perrin, JC, Delmar — locked. Crissdalynn — intentionally none (no defined Mortis; kid still coming into herself)
- Session 1 fully scripted (9 scenes), ready to run the moment Session 0 closes

**Gaps to close today:**

1. **Stripes** — no interview, no gravity wells, no Mortis, player TBD. Run section 4 separately before Session 1.
2. **Lines and veils** — establish and record today.
3. **Table expectations** — verbal is fine; cover it.

---

## Agenda

### 1. Table Talk (15–20 min)

**Tone and content**

- Lines (won't appear at all): ask each player. Common candidates: sexual violence, child harm.
- Veils (happens off-screen): torture details, extreme body horror. Confirm or adjust.
- X-card: always on the table. No explanation needed, no questions asked.

**Table expectations**

- Phones: call it.
- Attendance: how many to run? Cancellation window?
- "It's not working" signal: how does a player flag something without killing the session?

**Death rules** (in primer — confirm verbally)

- Death is on the table. DM won't aim for it but won't pad it.
- Options: resurrection or new same-level character.

---

### 2. Campaign Pitch (10 min)

Don't recite the primer. Hit the tone in one sentence:

> *Swashbuckling sophistication complicated by pettiness. Real stakes, stupid triggers, stylish people behaving badly.*

Then: **Archer but Age of Sail high magic.**

Confirm everyone has answered the four pre-session questions:

- Why are you aboard the Saltwright?
- What do you want badly enough to cross dangerous water for?
- What kind of trouble follows you onto a ship?
- What would make you stay with a crew when leaving would be easier?

---

### 3. Character Check-ins (20–30 min, established PCs)

Quick pass on Perrin, JC, Delmar, Crissdalynn. You have the gravity wells — this is a confirm, not an interview.

**For each:** "Tell me one thing your character wants right now and one thing they're afraid of losing." Listen for anything that contradicts or updates the gravity well notes.

Watch for:

- **Perrin + Crissdalynn friction** — prey response to large birds. Confirm Kaden knows this is a live dynamic.
- **JC's slave-catcher secret** — confirm Chad is comfortable with it surfacing mid-campaign as a grenade.
- **Delmar's five captains** — confirm Frederick knows this is an obsession, not a long game.
- **Crissdalynn's pilgrimage** — Drowned Maw convergence; player knows it points the same direction as Delmar's mission.

---

### 4. Stripes Interview — Full Session Zero (30–40 min)

> [!warning] Stripes not present at Session 0
> Run separately before Session 1. The whole profile is blank.

**Opening:** *"Tell me about Stripes — not the stats, the person. What do they look like and what's the first thing someone notices?"*

**Questions from [[character-interview-guide|Character Interview Guide]]:**

*Who they are:*

- What do they want right now?
- What are they afraid of losing?
- What do they believe that most people would disagree with?
- What's a line they won't cross?

*Where they've been:*

- What did their life look like before all this?
- What's the worst thing that's ever happened to them?
- What's the worst thing they've ever done?

*For the DM:*

- Give me one person from their past I can bring back — name, relationship, good or bad reunion?
- Give me one thing they want badly enough to do something questionable for.
- Give me one secret.
- Is there anything you want to explore through this character?

**Umberlee hook — probe specifically:**
Three other PCs have direct Umberlee entanglement. Stripes is described as a shrine guardian whose goal is to "set the seas right."

- What does "setting the seas right" mean to them specifically?
- What do they think is wrong?
- Does Umberlee speak to them, or is it one-way devotion?

**After the interview, extract:** Two Dials, Terminal Node, Active Friction → file to [[player-gravity-wells|Player Gravity Wells]].

---

### 5. Mortis for Stripes (10 min)

> [!warning] Deferred — run with section 4 above

> *"A Mark and a Gift — both describe the same person. The Mark must hurt. The Gift must feel like you."*

**Current party Mortises:**

| PC | Mark | Gift |
|---|---|---|
| Perrin | Disadv. all Str checks/saves | +2 Charisma |
| JC | Disadv. Persuasion + Deception | Adv. Perception + Survival |
| Delmar | Disadv. all Wis saves; captain surfacing triggers involuntary | Surface 1 captain 1/short rest (bonus action): 2 skills, Expertise if proficient |
| Crissdalynn | None | None |
| Stripes | TBD | TBD |

Process: player names the flaw → translate to mechanical condition → propose a Gift that exceeds the Mark → lock it in. DM has final say on both sides.

See [[mortis|The Mortis]] for design rules.

---

### 6. Player Goals — Round Table (10–15 min)

Ask the player, not the character:

1. What is your character trying to *become* by the end of this campaign?
2. What are they *afraid* of losing?
3. Who do they love, or who did they love?
4. What does failure look like for them personally?
5. What "red button" makes them throw caution to the wind?

---

### 7. Party Connection (10 min)

Everyone's aboard the Saltwright. Establish:

- Which PCs have history before this voyage?
- Which are strangers?
- Is there anyone who doesn't want to be here?

Enough so that [[session-01-scene-07-the-hold|Scene 07 — The Hold]] plays naturally.

---

## Close

If time allows, deliver the opening image:

> [!read-aloud]
> Two-masted merchant brig, riding low and cargo-heavy, moving slow through warm salt air. The northwestern Midchain. Stars from horizon to horizon. The sun went down an hour ago.

That's where they wake up in Session 1.

---

Before notes go stale:

- Stripes' gravity wells → [[player-gravity-wells|Player Gravity Wells]]
- Stripes' Mortis → section 5 table above
- Lines and veils for this table
- Any player goal answers that surprised you
- Party connection — who knows whom

# 01 — The Boarding of the Saltwright

---

The hold of the [[saltwright|Saltwright]] was dark and close, smelling of bilge water, shrimp, and the party waited in it like a held breath. Above, they could hear [[beaumont-sel|Beaumont]]'s voice carrying across the deck, easy and unhurried, keeping [[barnaby-rook|Barnaby Rook]]'s attention fixed at the wheel while three of his crew descended the ladder into the dark below.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-01-hold-waiting.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen cinematic scene inside the Saltwright's cramped cargo hold, old grey-brown two-masted merchant brig interior with stacked barrels, crates, sacks, two swinging lanterns, wet cedar beams, bilge-water sheen, and a narrow sliver of daylight through an aft gap above the waterline; Delmar Fisk waits with a musket, sandy red hair in a messy topknot, thick sandy-red beard and curled moustache with grey edges, salt-stiff scarlet admiral coat with gold epaulettes; Crissdalynn Khinriss crouches as a dark blue-black crow aarakocra monk with folded wings, talons, geometric leatherwork, and chart satchel; Perrin Black-Jaw hides as a very small three-foot black-and-white fancy-rat Rattkin sailor in an olive-drab hooded cloak, cream shirt, bodhran drum, long pink tail, and oversized longsword; Jean-Claude Tabarnack is a three-foot lean humanoid poison dart frog scaled to adventurer size, electric-blue slick skin, long thin frog limbs, splayed adhesive fingers and toes, large black underside patches, geometric black bands across arms, legs, shoulders, and face, red beret, false black moustache, ranger harness, shortbow and quiver, small scars, hard escaped-hunter stare, gripping a compact metal Flask of Endless Water; clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded lantern lighting, no text]]

The Enforcer came first. The crew had taken to calling him Cap'n Gorgeous, and the name wasn't wrong. Tall, broadly built, golden hair that caught even the thin light of the hold. He walked in without hesitation. The combined assault of a poisoned arrow from [[jean-claude-tabarnack|Jean-Claude]], a [[flask-of-endless-water|musket]] shot, and shattered knee cap answered him. The crack of black powder in that enclosed space was enormous, and for a ringing, disorienting moment both [[delmar-fisk|Delmar]] and [[crissdalynn-khinriss|Crissdalynn]] lost the world to white noise. The alarm went up. But [[perrin-black-jaw|Perrin]] had laid a Minor Illusion across the doorway they were sheltering behind, and Crissdalynn worked fast, dragging Cap'n Gorgeous back through it before the sound could be placed. The two deckhands came down cautious, uncertain, not knowing exactly what they were walking toward. They found out. Neither of them made it back up.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-02-capn-gorgeous-ambush.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen action scene in the dim cargo hold of the Saltwright, Cap'n Gorgeous the Dravosi enforcer has just stepped off the ladder into ambush, tall athletic human with long golden hair, coin-worthy jawline, pale blue eyes, dark Crown naval coat, and heavy crossbow; Delmar Fisk fires from the shadows with sandy red topknot, thick sandy-red beard and curled moustache, scarlet admiral coat, and musket flash filling the tight hold with smoke; Crissdalynn Khinriss, a dark blue-black crow aarakocra monk, moves fast to drag the fallen enforcer back through Perrin Black-Jaw's subtle purple Minor Illusion doorway; cramped barrels and rope everywhere, clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded lantern light, no gore, no text]]

Delmar knelt at the foot of the ladder and Crissdalynn didn't slow down. She hit his hands at a run and he launched her up through the hatch like a crack of thunder. Her wings snapped open the moment she cleared the weather deck and sent the two nearest Dravosi sprawling. Perrin and Jean-Claude emerged through a gap in the decking at a second angle, catching the remaining crew between them. It was over quickly. Both Dravosi Enforcers died in the press of it.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-03-crisdalynn-breach.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen deck fight on the Saltwright weather deck under grey Midchain light, Delmar Fisk with sandy red topknot and thick sandy-red beard braces at the hatch in a scarlet admiral coat after launching Crissdalynn Khinriss upward; Crissdalynn explodes through the opening as a dark blue-black crow aarakocra monk with wings snapping wide, talons forward, geometric leatherwork, and chart satchel, knocking two navy-blue Dravosi sailors with brass buttons sprawling across wet planks; Perrin Black-Jaw, a very small three-foot black-and-white fancy-rat Rattkin in an olive-drab hooded cloak with pink ears, long pink tail, bodhran, cream shirt, and oversized longsword, and Jean-Claude Tabarnack, a three-foot lean electric-blue humanoid poison dart frog with long thin limbs, splayed adhesive fingers and toes, large black underside patches, geometric black bands, red beret, false black moustache, ranger harness, shortbow and quiver, emerge from a second deck gap with hunter readiness; old plain merchant brig details, patched rail, working rigging, low deckhouse aft, clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded storm light, no text]]

When the last Dravosi deckhand, a young man maybe nineteen with frightened eyes, dropped his sword and went still, Rook's voice cut across the deck from the gangplank.

*"I'll shoot you myself for that, you turncoat."*

Delmar looked at the boy. "Would you rather fight for men who'll threaten to shoot you, or men who'll protect you?"

[[geoffrey-draves|Geoffrey Draves]] thought about it for about as long as it took him to answer. *"I'll do whatever keeps me alive today."*

He picked the sword back up and joined the fight. He is, by the current count, the party's entire crew.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-04-geoffrey-defects.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen tense character beat on the Saltwright deck after the boarding fight, Geoffrey Draves is a nineteen-year-old lean Dravosi deckhand and ship's carpenter in a dark privateer work shirt, frightened eyes, careful neutral expression, cutlass being returned; Delmar Fisk calmly offers the sword back with a knowing smile, sandy red hair in a topknot, thick sandy-red beard and curled moustache, salt-stiff scarlet admiral coat with gold epaulettes; Barnaby Rook threatens from the gangplank in the background in dark Crown officer clothing; fallen Crown sailors and scattered boarding hooks around them but no gore; HCS Surety is a small naval-grey patrol cutter with white waterline stripe and Crown pennant alongside; clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded overcast light, no text]]

The gangplank between the [[saltwright|Saltwright]] and the [[hcs-surety|HCS Surety]] was where things got complicated. Jean-Claude opened with the [[flask-of-endless-water|Flask of Endless Water]] and the blast caught Rook full in the chest, throwing him off the plank and buying the party precious seconds to deal with the Enforcer and the Alchemist before she could rejoin.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-05-gangplank-geyser.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen nautical action between the battered Saltwright merchant brig and the HCS Surety, a small low Dravosi Crown patrol cutter painted naval grey with a white stripe, brass registry plate, cannon amidships, and Crown pennant; Jean-Claude Tabarnack is a three-foot lean humanoid poison dart frog scaled to adventurer size, electric-blue slick skin, long thin frog limbs, splayed adhesive fingers and toes, large black underside patches, geometric black bands breaking up the vivid blue across his arms, legs, shoulders, and face, red beret and false black moustache, worn ranger harness, scars, compact shortbow and quiver, cool hard escaped-warrior posture as he braces both feet and unleashes the compact metal Flask of Endless Water in geyser mode; a violent jet of fresh water catches Barnaby Rook, hard Crown privateer captain in dark officer coat with flintlock and cutlass, square in the chest and throws him backward off the narrow gangplank; clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded storm light, no text]]

The Enforcer fell. The Alchemist took enough punishment to make her desperate, and desperation made her reach for the new canister on her bandolier. The gas rolled out across the deck and caught Jean-Claude and Perrin both. They resisted it. [[crissdalynn-khinriss|Crissdalynn]] answered with Gust and sent the cloud rolling back toward the Alchemist.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-06-poison-canister.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen scene on the slick Saltwright deck beside the gangplank, a Dravosi Crown alchemist warrant officer with a practical compound bandolier throws a sealed poison gas canister that bursts into a rolling greenish toxic cloud; Jean-Claude Tabarnack is central, a three-foot lean humanoid poison dart frog scaled to adventurer size, electric-blue slick skin, long thin frog limbs, splayed adhesive fingers and toes, large black underside patches, geometric black bands breaking up the vivid blue across his arms, legs, shoulders, and face, red beret and false black moustache, worn ranger harness, compact shortbow and quiver, scars, cool hard escaped-warrior stare as he registers the toxin through his skin; Perrin Black-Jaw, a very small three-foot black-and-white fancy-rat Rattkin sailor in an olive-drab hooded cloak, cream shirt, bodhran, long pink tail, and oversized longsword, grimaces beside him; Crissdalynn Khinriss, a dark blue-black crow aarakocra monk, pushes the cloud back with Gust; Simone Tabarnack appears only as a subtle ghosted memory in the gas, a compact purple Grung soldier with fitted armor, spear, and precise posture; clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded storm light, no readable labels, no text]]

Jean-Claude placed it in the same moment the fumes reached him. The toxin was [[simone-tabarnack|Simone]]'s. Unmistakably hers. His sister is supplying the [[dravosi-crown|Dravosi Crown]] with [[grung-clans|Grung]]-made toxin, and the proof of it was drifting across the decking between two ships in the Shattered Sea. He said nothing. The fight continued.

The Alchemist was brought down. Rook hauled himself back over the rail, raised his flintlock at [[beaumont-sel|Beaumont]], and fired. The round struck the ridged plate of Beaumont's salvaged shell at his shoulder and spun away into the water.

![[sessions/session-art/session-01-07-beaumont-deflection.webp|Archer-style adult animated illustration, widescreen final beat on the Saltwright deck, Barnaby Rook hauls himself over the rail from the HCS Surety side in a dark Crown officer coat and fires a flintlock at Beaumont Sel; the bullet sparks off Beaumont's mirror-bright Salvaged Antheri Plate, a single dark Antheri-alloy pauldron fitted flush over the upper-right breach of his river-mud brown ridged tortle shell, ricocheting toward the sea; Beaumont is an old alligator-snapping tortle captain with sun-bleached leather eye cover, broad undershot jaw, short clay pipe, Bisou the capuchin clinging to his left shoulder, unhurried and unimpressed as he reaches for a boat hook; wet deck, Crown cutter beside old merchant brig, clean vector-like linework, cel-shaded storm light, no text]]

*"Boy, I shit out harder things than you every mornin'."*

That's where we left it.

# Beat 1: The World

*The Shattered Sea.*

*Sixty thousand square miles of reef and deep water, bounded on two sides by things that wreck ships. To the west: the [[galewall|Galewall]], a permanent storm belt the colonial homelands sit beyond. To the east: the [[the-drowned-maw|Drowned Maw]], a deep sea trench rumoured to be bottomless and causing compass needles to drift. Between them: two arcs of limestone and rainforest, hundreds of islands. And things that were here long before the first foreign flag went into the sand.*

*Two powers have spent three centuries deciding this sea belongs to them. The [[dravosi-crown|Dravosi Crown]] holds the northern arc in brass stamps and inspection seals. The [[tessarine-concordat|Tessarine Concordat]] does not conquer — it lends, and waits, and by the time a city notices, half its council is servicing Concordat debt. And beneath both, older than either, [[the-passage|the Passage]] — the [[rattkin|Rattkin]] network of routes and shelters running through every port's foundations. It does not appear on colonial charts. It does not ask permission. The Rattkin were here before the first ship arrived and have been inside every wall built since.*

*The one arrangement that has held, in every port, under every flag, is [[umberlee|Umberlee's]]. A shrine at every harbour mouth. Salt-bleached robes. A fee schedule in three languages. Pay and sail.*

*Five days ago, five ships went down together.*

*Tonight, the northwestern edge of [[midchain|the Midchain]] — the independent southern arc, low limestone islands, free ports where fishing villages and smuggling routes share the same docks.*

*The sun went down an hour ago. The air is warm and salt-heavy, thick with the sweetness of rainforest rot drifting off the water. Stars from horizon to horizon. Somewhere in the trees to port, something calls once, and stops.*

Beat 1: The World

The Shattered Sea.

Sixty thousand square miles of reef and deep water, bounded on two sides by things that wreck ships. To the west: the Galewall, a permanent storm belt the colonial homelands sit beyond. To the east: the Drowned Maw, a deep sea trench rumoured to be bottomless and causing compass needles to drift. Between them: two arcs of limestone and rainforest, hundreds of islands. And things that were here long before the first foreign flag went into the sand.

Two powers have spent three centuries deciding this sea belongs to them. The Dravosi Crown holds the northern arc in brass stamps and inspection seals. The Tessarine Concordat does not conquer — it lends, and waits, and by the time a city notices, half its council is servicing Concordat debt. And beneath both, older than either, the Passage — the Rattkin network of routes and shelters running through every port’s foundations. It does not appear on colonial charts. It does not ask permission. The Rattkin were here before the first ship arrived and have been inside every wall built since.

The one arrangement that has held, in every port, under every flag, is Umberlee’s. A shrine at every harbour mouth. Salt-bleached robes. A fee schedule in three languages. Pay and sail.

Five days ago, five ships went down together.

# Beat 2: Crissdalynn

*(Address Crissdalynn.)*

*The wind finds you at forty feet, pressing under your wings in long even pulses. Below you, the [[saltwright|Saltwright]] moves slow through the channel, cargo-heavy, her lanterns swaying. The sea spreads wide in every direction, and it is calm. Not peaceful.*

*The [[high-eyrie|High Eyrie]] trained you to record exactly what you see. Every [[sentinels-of-the-eyrie|Sentinel]] who comes out of that basalt rock carries two things: the discipline to observe without flinching, and a task their master set before sending them into the world. Not a suggestion. A task. Your master [[master-kyzil|Kyzil]] sent you to map the [[the-drowned-maw|Drowned Maw]] from inside a storm — a task given at fourteen, after he caught you flying lazy circles when you should have been at your post.*

*You were close. Two years aboard the [[red-lady|Red Lady]] with [[delmar-fisk|Delmar Fisk's]] fleet, the charts in your satchel filling in slowly, the Maw mapped to its southern arc and most of its eastern rim. Then five days ago the Maw opened, and all five ships went down together. You pulled Fisk clear and the two of you surfaced among the wreckage. The rest did not.*

*The [[saltwright|Saltwright]] found you two days ago. The charts are still in the satchel.*

*Could you describe what they see — the Saltwright from up here, the channel ahead, the dark?*

[Let her go. When she settles:]

*At the wheel below stands the Tortle captain who found you and Fisk on the driftwood two days ago and pulled you aboard without a question or a second thought.*

*He goes by Beaumont. An old alligator snapping Tortle, shell the colour of river mud and heavily ridged — fist-sized metal plate bolted to the upper-right panel, chipped spike where something landed hard once. One eye patched in sun-bleached leather. On his left shoulder, a small monkey called [[bisou|Bisou]] treats the theft of his pipe as a full-time occupation.*

**Beaumont**: *"Mais. Anything on the water to the east? Current runs strange past the reef."*

> [!check] Perception — The cutter
> Flavour only — there is a cutter regardless of the result.
> DC 12: A Dravosi patrol cutter, running slow. Standard configuration — nothing obviously wrong from up here.
> DC 16: In poor wear and maintenance — chipped paint, one running light out, rigging not quite right. Definitely not standard-issue anymore. Moving on an intercept heading with the Saltwright, with the unhurried confidence of something that expects to be obeyed.

**Beaumont**: *"Mm. Probably just old Norrington, not to worry."*

[Give Crissdalynn a moment at the wheel. Beaumont is comfortable with silence — he doesn't fill it. If she asks about the route: three days past Kalowe, two past Aldenmere, Calder's Tooth still ahead. If she asks about Norrington: a shrug. *"Good man. Retired, apparently."* He doesn't believe it. If she pushes on the cutter's heading: *"Could be a drill. Crown runs them sometimes."* He lights his pipe. Bisou steals it. He takes it back without looking. He does not sound like a man who thinks this is a drill.]

*Beaumont's gaze stays on the channel. At the port rail, leaning into the dark, a man in a red Admiral's coat watches the same water — and has been, for a while.*

*(Address Delmar — see [[session-01-scene-03-delmar|Scene 03]].)*

# Beat 3: Delmar

*(Address Delmar.)*

*You have been leaning against that rail for ten minutes already. The night air is warm and thick with salt, and the [[saltwright|Saltwright]] moves slow beneath your feet. The red coat with the gold epaulettes — Admiral's colours.*

*Five days ago you were commanding five ships into the [[sunken-crown|Sunken Crown]] on commission from the [[chain-council|Chain Council]]. A benefactor had come to the Council with a proposition: lift a relic from a shrine on [[vel-orn|Vel Orn]] and it would protect the Midchain waters from her wrath. The Council believed it. They hired you. You went in clean, lifted the [[pearl-of-souls|Pearl]], and made the outbound tide.*

*Then the [[the-drowned-maw|Maw]] opened. The name proved true — a chasm, wide and deep, and all five ships gone before anyone understood what was happening. You heard voices as the hull came apart around you. You'd be dead in that water if not for [[crissdalynn-khinriss|Crissdalynn]], who found you in the wreckage and got you onto driftwood. The [[saltwright|Saltwright]] found you both two days later.*

*Could you tell us about who we see leaning on that rail?*

[Let them finish.]

*The night has been quiet. Then [[bisou|Bisou]] — Beaumont's monkey — noticed the coin you've been turning between your fingers.*

*[[bisou|Bisou]] has been on your arm for three minutes now, slack-jawed.*

*Every time he reaches for the coin, the coin is somewhere else. Between two fingers. Gone. The other hand. Gone again. Bisou lunges, misses, makes a sound, and tries again.*

> [!check] Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) — The coin trick
> Flavour only — Bisou is not getting the coin. The result determines how decisively Delmar wins.
> DC 10: Bisou tracks the correct hand. It knows. Sits with one finger pointed at Fisk's closed fist, not lunging anymore, just waiting with immovable certainty. From the wheel, Beaumont's shoulders are shaking.
> DC 15: Bisou stares at both hands. Then at Fisk's face. Then back at the hands. Makes a low, baffled sound, like a question asked of no one in particular.
> DC 20: Bisou looks at both hands. Looks at Fisk. Then with great dignity turns its back, tucks its chin, and refuses to acknowledge that any of this is happening. It has decided the coin does not exist. From the wheel, Beaumont is no longer pretending not to watch.

**Beaumont**: *"Bisou. Leave the man alone, cher."*

[Bisou retreats — pointedly, toward the pocket the coin disappeared into. If Delmar asks Beaumont about the cutter: *"Probably just Norrington."* If he pushes — and a man who commanded five ships probably will — Beaumont gives him a look and a shrug. *"Different face on the same route."* He won't say more out here. Deck goes quiet.]

*Along the rail toward the bow, the rest of the deck has been running a different competition for the last hour. Spears and lines. No one winning yet.*

*(Address Stripes — see [[session-01-scene-04-stripes|Scene 04]].)*

# Beat 4: Stripes

*(Address Stripes.)*

*You're on a stranger's ship in the dark. The salt air is warm, the Midchain sliding past on both sides of the hull, and you are here simply because [[elder-anton|Elder Anton]] asked you to go.*

*[[stripes-bitemore|Stripes Bitemore]] — the greatest hunter of [[keth-naar|Keth-Naar]]. Twelve black basalt promontories jutting from pale water, sharp as cut stone, worn smooth where your people have walked them for generations. The channels run so clear you can see thirty feet down. At dawn the keth-fin hold position in the current, thick and silver-flanked, and your people take what they need.*

*Five days ago the keth-fin scattered. The birds fled in great flocks. The water brought a new foul smell up from the deep. The Elders gathered, and Anton — the strongest among them — sent his apprentice out into the Midchain to find the cause.*

*Could you show us what they see — who is standing on that rail?*

[Let them finish.]

*The crew has been at this for an hour and has nothing yet. Close to the hull, two feet down, a school of yellowtail snapper holds position in the [[saltwright|Saltwright's]] shadow — the kind that gathers under hulls to feed on what falls over the side. Not keth-fin. Smaller, shallower. But they are there, and they are close.*

> This roll is flavour only — Stripes takes a fish. The result determines by how much he wins.
